source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) Analogical mapping by constraint satisfaction (ACME)
finding: ACME maps by parallel constraint satisfaction over structural, semantic and pragmatic constraints. It found the mappings on the radiation/lightbulb convergence analogy in all four surface versions. It breaks down where humans fail: in the poor-constraint versions the key proposition (do not destroy healthy tissue) has no counterpart to map to.
numbers: Laser/fragile-glass network settled at cycle 31 (192 units, 1773 links). Cycles to success barely differ by surface similarity. Human data from Holyoak & Koh 1987 (solutions after hint roughly 75% in good-constraint vs 47-60% in poor-constraint versions; the OCR of Table 5 is garbled, treat exact cells as approximate).
limits: Only qualitative fit to the human ordering. Source and target are handed to the model (no retrieval). Small hand-built predicate-calculus inputs.
agent_relevance: Mapping fails exactly when a decisive constraint has no partner. Before trusting an analogy, our agent should check that the key constraint of the problem has a mapped counterpart.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) ACME parameter sensitivity on cross-mapped stories (Table 15, Gentner & Toupin materials)
finding: On cross-mapped unsystematic stories (similar objects in different roles) ACME did not settle on the correct mapping. It succeeded only after retuning inhibition or the minimum-activation parameter. Systematicity only helped in the cross-mapped condition.
numbers: Cycles to success: easy conditions about 3-4, cross-mapped systematic 38, cross-mapped unsystematic no success. Fix: change inhibition from -.2 to -.1, or min from -1 to -.3. Humans (Gentner & Toupin 1986): cross-mapped is hardest; younger children gain less from systematicity.
limits: ACME showed a smaller same-vs-different-domain gap than Gentner & Toupin's subjects. Parameter-fragile on the exact case where surface similarity misleads.
agent_relevance: The hard case for any mapper is surface lure vs role match. Map roles first, and compare surface similarity second, when they conflict.

source: Holyoak & Thagard (1989) ACME compared with SME and Copycat
finding: The authors state ACME extends SME: pragmatic and semantic constraints act during mapping and structure is a soft pressure, not a hard filter. ACME can map from isomorphism alone, with no semantic overlap (boys-dogs problem).
numbers: Boys-dogs problem: ACME solves it by isomorphism alone. Holyoak & Thagard report 6 of 8 college students gave all six correct mappings within 3 min (as cited in Hummel & Holyoak 1997).
limits: Comparison with SME is by argument and example, not a matched human experiment.
agent_relevance: Soft structural pressure plus explicit goal weighting is a usable design for a mapping step. Hard systematicity alone can miss goal-relevant matches.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) Distributed representations of structure: LISA
finding: LISA uses temporal-synchrony binding over a distributed semantic code, so one architecture does access, mapping and inference. Working memory is capped at about 4-6 role bindings, so large analogies are mapped in small sequential pieces. The authors argue ACME and SME are too powerful compared with humans.
numbers: Phase set 4-6 role bindings (about 25 ms period, 5 ms phases). Simulations use small hand-built examples; the model is stochastic and sensitive to proposition order. Written on a 486 PC; scale-up explicitly not tested.
limits: Qualitative fit only (signs of ordinal contrasts), not quantitative.
agent_relevance: A human-like capacity limit on parallel mapping is a feature. Our scaffold can map in small chunks (3-5 relations at a time) instead of the whole domain at once.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) critique of ACME: over-powerful on unnatural mappings (Keane et al. 1994 data)
finding: ACME solves the unnatural boys-dogs mapping in parallel as easily as natural ones. People do not. They re-represent the analogs (noticing one property vs two) and step through serial hypotheses like a puzzle.
numbers: Holyoak & Thagard: 6 of 8 students correct within 3 min. Keane et al. 1994: about 3-6 min with experimenter feedback on each error.
limits: Partly based on the authors' informal observation. Keane et al. 1994 was not opened (secondhand).
agent_relevance: When the mapping is arbitrary, humans use serial hypothesis testing with error checks. The agent should do the same: propose, test, backtrack.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) LISA on Ross (1987, 1989) access vs mapping dissociation
finding: Humans: object similarity in matching roles helps both retrieval and mapping, but the pattern differs between them. LISA reproduced the signs of the four ordinal contrasts with one set of connections.
limits: Magnitudes differ by up to ten times on mapping. Only the direction matches. Ross data are word problems with college students.
agent_relevance: Retrieval is driven by surface and story similarity. Mapping is driven by role consistency. Do not use one similarity score for both steps.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (2003) A symbolic-connectionist theory of relational inference and generalization
finding: Extends LISA to inference and schema induction. An inference is made only if at least 70% of the importance-weighted structure is mapped. At most three propositions fit in working memory (4-6 role bindings). Inferences vary from run to run when constraints are weak.
numbers: Lassaline (1996) simulation, 50 runs each. Medium constraint: both inferences on 15 runs, weak-immune-only 11, partial 13, none 11. The weak-constraint condition gave the fewest inferences.
limits: Qualitative simulations of a handful of studies. Many free parameters (importance values, thresholds).
agent_relevance: Gate analogical inference on mapping coverage (a threshold like 70%) and mark inferences from weak mappings as tentative.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) LISA retrieval index: Weber fraction with Luce competition
finding: Retrieval index uses a Weber fraction of summed activation so short and long analogs compete fairly, plus Luce choice competition. Wharton et al. (1991) found human retrieval fits the Luce model.
numbers: Raw index R about 0.01-2.00; Luce index L = R divided by sum of R over analogs.
limits: Wharton et al. 1991 not opened (secondhand).
agent_relevance: Rank candidate sources with normalised competition, not raw match counts, so long sources do not dominate.

source: Hummel & Holyoak (1997) list of limits of ACME/SME-class models
finding: Four doubts about earlier models: no working-memory limit, no joint account of access and mapping, over- and under-powerful mapping (n-ary restriction), and no learning of schemas.
numbers: Qualitative list; Table 1 lists 14 phenomena to be explained.
limits: Written by the LISA authors to motivate their own model.
agent_relevance: A checklist for the mapping step: capacity limit, joint access and mapping, flexible arity, schema learning after success.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on digit matrices, letter strings and verbal analogies. College students beat it on story analogies, especially far analogies.
numbers: Digit matrices: generative OR 1.88 (p=.005), multiple choice OR 6.27 (humans N=40). Letter strings OR 1.76 (p=6.3e-5; N=57). Story analogies OR 0.37 (p=.0003) favouring humans (N=54; 15/54 humans right on every trial). GPT-3 far-analogy binomial p=.065, not above chance.
limits: Items may be in training data. Humans were UCLA undergraduates. Zero-shot, one model. Contested later (b12-b16).
agent_relevance: The best-known positive result for LLM mapping, but far story mapping was the weak spot, the part our agent needs most.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) account of why transformers can map
finding: Authors link self-attention to the pairwise similarity step of ACME/LISA mapping, and key/value indirection to variable binding. They also warn LLMs may be a different kind of intelligence.
numbers: Not an experiment. No ablation reported.
limits: Speculative mechanism. Later work found brittleness on counterfactual variants.
agent_relevance: An LLM may do the soft-similarity half of mapping, not necessarily the binding half. The scaffold should supply an explicit binding table.

source: Hodel & West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Simple counterfactual changes broke GPT-3 on letter-string tasks (synthetic alphabet in the prompt, larger intervals). Humans stayed high.
numbers: GPT-3 generative accuracy on the synthetic alphabet below 0.1 for extend-sequence, successor/predecessor and fix-alphabet. Only remove-redundant and sort stayed near the original range.
limits: Preprint, GPT-3 only. Counting and prompt format may explain part of the drop (see b16).
agent_relevance: Mapping that leans on memorised sequences will not transfer. Test the mapper on perturbed versions of each problem.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs
finding: Replicated Webb's letter-string results. GPT models were below humans on the original problems and worse on permuted and symbol alphabets. Humans were stable across alphabets.
numbers: Counterfactual problems, all alphabets: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773] (1876 samples, 136 Prolific recruits); GPT-3 0.488; GPT-3.5 0.350; GPT-4 0.452 (6840 samples each). Human errors: 38.59% alternative-rule; GPT-4 22%; GPT-3 5.81%.
limits: Humans scored higher than in Webb's sample. Prompt-format sensitive. Counterfactual comprehension checks mostly passed.
agent_relevance: LLM analogy scores partly rest on familiar content. The scaffold should abstract the relation from surface form before mapping.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2025) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs: matrices and answer order
finding: Digit matrices: GPT drops only for the alternate-blank variant. Stories: strong answer-order bias in GPT-4.
numbers: Digit matrices (digits / alternate blank / symbols): humans 0.715 / 0.771 / 0.704; GPT-4 about 0.81 / 0.48 / 0.79 (row labels garbled in the text extraction; ordering inferred from the abstract). Story answer order for GPT-4: 89% (16/18) when story A correct vs 61% (11/18) when B correct.
limits: PDF table layout ambiguous; check the TMLR version before quoting cells.
agent_relevance: Randomise option order and test both orders for every mapping judgment. A 28-point order effect is large.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2025) paraphrase test of story-analogy shortcuts
finding: Correct target stories often shared sentence-level structure with the source. Rewriting only the correct target to remove that overlap hurt GPT-4 about twice as much as humans.
numbers: GPT-4 86% to 72% (original to paraphrased). Humans 78% to 70% (reported in Inani et al. 2025, citing this work).
limits: 18 stories only. Human numbers from a secondary citation.
agent_relevance: Surface alignment can pass as relational mapping. Require explicit role-correspondence evidence, not overall story similarity.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning
finding: Reply to both critiques: counterfactual failure comes from counting letters in the permuted alphabet. GPT-4 with code execution solved permuted-alphabet problems at human level.
numbers: Humans N=99 (interval 1), N=97 (interval 2). Human vs GPT-4: P=8.9e-13 (humans better). Human vs GPT-4 + code: P=0.496 (no difference). 46% of GPT-4 errors used a valid alternative rule vs 39% for humans.
limits: Code execution is not human-like. Only letter-string counterfactuals. A reply by the original authors, not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: A rival explanation that matters: give the agent tools for non-relational substeps (counting, lookup) so they are not mistaken for mapping failure.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can?
finding: Adults and 7-9 year-olds kept their score across Latin, Greek and symbol alphabets. All four LLMs got worse, most in the far (symbol) domain.
numbers: Accuracy Latin/Greek/Symbol: adults 0.88/0.91/0.89 (N=62); children 0.62/0.66/0.67 (N=41); GPT-4o 0.85/0.63/0.48; Claude-3.5 0.68/0.62/0.46; Llama-3.1 405B 0.79/0.74/0.27; Gemma-2 27B 0.60/0.39/0.14. Alphabet effect adults n.s. (F=0.95); each LLM p<.001.
limits: Letter strings only; no reasoning-tuned models. A separate next/previous check showed the models knew successor and predecessor. Hardest items for people and LLMs: predecessor and second-successor.
agent_relevance: Near-to-far transfer is where the model loses ground. Far mappings need an explicit relation-extraction step before comparison.

source: Mitchell, Palmarini & Moskvichev (2023) Comparing humans, GPT-4 and GPT-4V on abstraction and reasoning tasks
finding: On ConceptARC (480 tasks) humans far exceeded programs and GPT-4. A more detailed one-shot prompt helped GPT-4 but did not close the gap.
numbers: Humans 91%, first-place Kaggle program 52%, GPT-4 25% (temp 0.5). One-shot prompt: GPT-4 0.33 at both temperatures vs 0.19 (temp 0) and 0.25 (temp 0.5) zero-shot. GPT-4V visual one-shot 0.23 on 48 minimal tasks; text 0.25.
limits: 2023 models. GPT-4V test was small (48 tasks).
agent_relevance: A mapping-like abstraction task where plain prompting gives about a third of human accuracy. Good benchmark for the scaffold.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard & Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC benchmark
finding: 16 concept groups, 30 test inputs each. Humans scored 83-97% per group, GPT-4 3-33%.
numbers: Human vs GPT-4 by group: Count 0.86 vs 0.03; Copy 0.93 vs 0.07; Center 0.97 vs 0.20; Inside/Outside 0.83 vs 0.27. Kaggle first place 0.23-0.77.
limits: Some rows misaligned in the text extraction; group-level pattern is robust.
agent_relevance: Counting and copying were worst for the LLM, the same non-relational substep problem as b16.

source: Gendron, Bao, Witbrock & Dobbie (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: New abstract-reasoning benchmark. LLMs score very low compared with other NLP tasks, even with chain of thought and few-shot techniques.
numbers: Exact scores not read (abstract only).
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read. Do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Supports not relying on prompting tricks alone for abstract mapping.

source: Mitchell (2021) Abstraction and analogy-making in artificial intelligence: hybrid models and Copycat
finding: Hybrid models (ACME, LISA) handle mapping but need hand-built representations. Copycat's concept network was built by hand, it is handed a source and target, and its parameter tuning is ad hoc. No system learns new permanent concepts.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Review by a Copycat author; may favour Copycat.
agent_relevance: Representation building is the bottleneck for every mapping model. Our agent has an LLM for that, which is the new ingredient.

source: Mitchell (2021) on interpretation and mapping interacting
finding: SME-style systems leave out how a situation is understood and how interpretation interacts with mapping. Copycat builds its representation inside the mapping loop.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument, not experiment.
agent_relevance: Interleave re-description and mapping. After a failed mapping, let the agent re-represent the source, as in the Copycat loop and the human boys-dogs strategy.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners
finding: Prompting the LLM to self-generate relevant examples (and knowledge) before solving beat 0-shot and few-shot chain of thought on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench.
numbers: Average gain about +4% over baselines across GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and PaLM2. K=5 self-generated exemplars for GSM8K, K=3 for MATH and BIG-Bench. Single table cells garbled in extraction, not recorded.
limits: Analogy as retrieval by prompting; no explicit mapping step. Gains are modest. Contamination not ruled out.
agent_relevance: A cheap analogical-retrieval step to add before reasoning. Test whether adding explicit role mapping improves on it.

source: Webb, Frankland et al. (2024) The relational bottleneck as an inductive bias for efficient abstraction
finding: Reviews models that force networks to attend to relations between inputs rather than input attributes, as a reconciliation of connectionist and symbolic accounts.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract and introduction only).
limits: Abstract level only.
agent_relevance: The architecture version of what our scaffold imposes by prompt: ask for relations first, attributes second.

source: Webb, Sinha & Cohen (2021) Emergent symbols through binding in external memory (ESBN)
finding: A recurrent net with external memory that separates variable keys from values learned rules that generalised almost perfectly to novel entities.
numbers: Abstract only: nearly perfect generalization on rule tasks; exact numbers not read.
limits: Abstract only; small synthetic tasks.
agent_relevance: Variable binding via an explicit memory is what LISA does by synchrony. A written role-binding table in the scaffold plays that role for an LLM.

source: Inani, Kabra, Marupudi & Varma (2025) Modeling understanding of story-based analogies using LLMs
finding: On the 18 Gentner-style story analogies, bigger models score as high as or above humans, but their per-item difficulty profile does not track humans well.
numbers: Humans 0.847; GPT-3 0.75; Llama-3.1 70B 0.8538 vs 8B 0.6528; GPT-4o 0.8233 vs mini 0.7011 (about 15 points per size step). Item-level correlation with humans: BERT embedding r=-0.032 (p=.899); best model r=0.526 (p=.025). Embedding similarity picked the right story 78% of the time.
limits: A self-hint prompt raised accuracy for some models but lowered human correlation (table cells garbled; only direction safe). Published stories may be in training data.
agent_relevance: High accuracy with a different difficulty profile suggests different cues. Check by item, not by the mean.
